## Simple explanation

Clustering groups data points that appear similar, without requiring a
known label for every point. The groups can help explore structure in
data, but their meaning often requires human interpretation.

## Technical explanation

Clustering algorithms define similarity or density and produce group
assignments, sometimes with a noise or outlier category. Methods include
k-means, hierarchical clustering, and density-based algorithms. Results
depend on feature representation, scaling, distance measure, and algorithm
assumptions.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Clustering can support exploration, segmentation, deduplication, and
organization of embeddings. Since there may be no ground-truth labels,
engineers should inspect cluster quality, stability, and usefulness for
the intended downstream task.

## How it works

An algorithm compares examples using a distance, density, or other
similarity notion and assigns or organizes them into groups. Some methods
require a chosen number of clusters; others infer groups from local
density. Feature preprocessing can substantially change the result.

## Practical example

A team can cluster text embeddings of support tickets to discover common
themes. Human reviewers can inspect representative tickets to determine
whether the clusters correspond to meaningful categories.

## Common misconceptions

- Clusters discovered by an algorithm are not automatically real or
  meaningful categories.
- Different algorithms or feature scaling can produce different groupings.
- Clustering does not replace classification when reliable labels and a
  prediction task are available.
